FOREWORD 


This Indian Standard (First Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards after the draft finalized 
by the Agriculture and Food Processing Equipment Sectional Committee had been approved by the Food and 
Agriculture Division Council. 


This standard was first published in 2008. The first revision has been taken up to keep pace with the latest 
technological developments and international practices. 


In this revision following major changes have been made: 
a) Scope, 
b) Material specification, 
c) Test methods has been updated, 
d) Types of cladding film based properties have been added, and 
e) Technical data sheet for various types of film is provided. 
In the formulation of this standard, considerable assistance has been derived from the following International 
Standard: 
BS EN 13206 : 2017 Plastics — Thermoplastic covering films for use in agriculture and horticulture 


The composition of the Committee, responsible for the formulation of this standard is given at Annex A. 


For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with the final value, 
observed or calculated expressing the result of a test or analysis shall be rounded off in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 
‘Rules for rounding off numerical values (revised ).’ The number of significant places retained in the rounded off 
value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard. 


IS 15827 : 2019 


Indian Standard 


CLADDING FILMS FOR GREENHOUSE/ 
POLY HOUSE — SPECIFICATIONS 


( First Revision ) 


1 SCOPE 


This standard specifies requirements and their test 
methods for UV stabilized multi-layered cladding films 
for greenhouse / polyhouse. 


2 REFERENCES 


The following standards contain provisions, which 
through reference in this text, constitute provisions of 
this standard. At the time of publication, the editions 
indicated were valid. All standards are subject to 
revision and parties to agreements based on this 
standard are encouraged to investigate the possibility 
of applying the most recent editions of the standards 
indicated below:

3 TERMINOLOGY 


3.1 Absorptance — Ability of a material to absorb 
energy. 


3.2. Actual Yield — It is the area provided by given 
mass of a film of specified thickness. 


3.3 Ageing — Gradual process in which the properties 
of a material, structure or system changes over time, 
usage, biological, chemical or through physical agents. 


3.4 Burn Rate — The relative rate and/or extent and 
time of burning of plastics. 


3.5 Coefficient of Expansion — The fractional change 
in length of a material for a unit change in temperature. 
That is, the number of mm expanded for each mm of 
total length when the temperature rises by 1°C. 


3.6 Composite — A plastic structure consisting of two 
or more different materials intimately mixed together. 


3.7 Copolymer — A plastic made by mixing two or 
more monomers, which polymerize together. 


3.8 Density — The mass of a material per unit volume. 


3.9 Diffused Radiation — Solar radiation received 
from the sun after its direction has been changed by 
reflection and scattering by the cladding material. 


3.10 Elasticity — The tendency of a material to return 
to its natural size and shape after removal of deforming 
load. 


3.11 Emittance — The energy radiated by the surface 
of a body per second per unit area. 


3.12 Elongation — The increase in length of a material 
being loaded in tension. 


3.13 Extrusion — Forcing conditioned raw material 
through a die to form a continuous shaped product. 


3.14 Flame-Resistive — Commonly, the property of 
materials that will improve its ability to resist ignition 
when exposed to flame. 


3.15 Flash Point — The lowest temperature at 
which a substance in an open vessel gives off enough 
combustible vapour to produce momentary ignition 
when a small flame is passed near its surface. 


3.16 Haze — The scattering of light by a specimen 
(cladding) responsible for the reduction in visibility of 
object viewed through it. 


IS 15827 : 2019 


3.17 Diffusion — It is the scattering of light by the 
specimen (cladding). 


3.18 Ignition Temperature — The temperature at 
which a material will start burning without an external 
flame (self-ignition temperature) and/or the temperature 
at which a material ignites in the presence of external 
flame (flash ignition temperature). 


3.19 Impact Resistance — The ability of the material 
to withstand a shock or sudden force. 


3.20 Impact Strength — The ability to resist breakage 
by flexural shock. 


3.21 Impact Failure Load — It is the load at which 50 
percent of the specimens fail when tested by the impact 
resistance method. 


3.22 Tearing Strength — The ability of a material to 
resist tearing. 


3.23 Tensile Strength — The ability of a material to 
resist being pulled apart. 


3.24 Specific Gravity — It is the ratio of the density 
of a substance to the density of a reference substance. 


3.25 Polymer — A long-chain compound made up of 
many repeating units joined together chemically. 


3.26 Plastic Material — Plastic may be any of 
numerous organic , synthetic or processed materials 
that are molded, cast , extruded, drawn or laminated 
into objects and films or filaments. 


3.27 Inhibitor — A substance that slows down and 
prevents chemical reaction. 


3.28 Plasticizer — A chemical substance added to 
plastic to make it softer and more flexible. 


3.29 UV Absorbers — A chemical compound with 
the ability to selectively absorb UV radiation. When 
incorporated into plastics it reduces the degrading 
effects of ultraviolet energy. 


3.30 UV Stabilizers — UV stabilizers are used 
frequently in plastics, including cosmetics and films. 
The primary function is to protect the substance from 
the long-term UV degradation effects from ultraviolet 
radiation. Different UV stabilizers are utilized 
depending upon the substrate, intended functional life, 
and sensitivity to UV degradation. 


3.31 Reinforcement — A strong material added to 
a base material to improve its strength, stiffness, and 
impact resistance. 


3.32 Self-extinguishing — The ability of a material 
to cease burning when the source of flame has been 
removed. 


3.33 Nominal Width — The theoretically desired width 
of a film for a particular application. It is declared by 
the manufacturer in meters at right angles to the length 
/ extrusion direction. 


3.34 Nominal Thickness — The theoretically desired 
thickness of a film for particular application and is 
declared by the manufacturer in microns. 


3.35 Length of the Roll — The largest dimension of 
the roll in meters in extrusion direction. 


3.36 Machine / Longitudinal Direction of the Roll 
(MD) — Parallel to the length of the roll corresponding 
to the extrusion direction. 


3.37 Transverse Direction of the Roll (TD) — The 
direction (parallel to the width) at right angles to the 
length / extrusion direction. 


3.38 Total Solar Radiation — It includes the entire 
available energy spectrum emitted by the sun. It 
includes the major energy carrier in the near infrared 
waveband and is useful in calculating total energy 
gain in a greenhouse so that heating and cooling 
requirements can be calculated. 


3.39 Transmission of Solar Energy — The percentage 
of total solar energy, which a cladding film allows to 
pass through itself. 


3.40 Light Transmission — The percentage of light 
(energy) passing through a cladding film. 


3.41 Thermal Radiation — The radiation emitted by 
a body as a result of its temperature (that is, thermal 
motion of its electrons). The spread of thermal radiation 
spectrum is from microwaves to x-rays depending upon 
temperature of the object. 


3.42 Reflectance — Energy that has not been 
transmitted or absorbed by cladding film. 


3.43 Shading Coefficient — The ratio of solar heat 
gain through a cladding material under a specific set 
of conditions. 


3.44 Ultraviolet Rays (UV) — It is invisible 
high energy radiation on the left hand of the solar 
spectrum that is 190 nm 400 nm. It is further divided 
as below: 

a) UVA — 315 to 400 nm; 

b) UV B — 280 to 315 nm; and 

c) UV C— 100 to 280 nm. 


3.45 Photosynthetic Active Radiation (PAR) — The 
visible portion of the solar radiation ranging from 
400 nm to 700 nm, which is critical for proper plant 
growth, development and photosynthesis, is called 
Photosynthetic Active Radiation (PAR). 


3.46 Infrared — Light on the long wave end of the 
spectrum which is invisible to the human eye but very 
penetrating. (Range 700 nm to 1,000 000 nm) of light 
(energy) allowed to pass through a material. This is part 
of the solar radiation, which adds to the heating of the 
greenhouse. It is further divided as below: 


a) Near Infrared Transmission (NIR) — (700 nm — 
1 100 nm); 


b) Mid Infrared Transmission (MIR) — (1 100 nm — 
1600 nm); and 


c) Far Infrared Transmission (FIR) — (1600 nm — 
1,000,000 nm). 


3.47 K Factor (Thermal Conductivity) — This factor 
indicates the amount of heat transferred in unit time 
through unit area of homogeneous material of unit 
thickness with a unit temperature difference between 
its two surfaces. 


3.48 Longevity — Usable life of cladding materials is 
defined as the period (the number of months or years) 
that a material will function effectively in commercial 
growing applications. To function effectively it must 
retain its essential properties of strength and inherent 
light transmission (that part owing to internal chemical 
change as opposed to that part owing to external 
factors such as accumulated dust, dirt and the effects of 
corrosive atmospheres). 


3.49 Weathering — The effects ona material of outdoor 
exposure including water. UV radiation, oxidation etc. 


3.50 Weatherometer — A device that measures the 
controlled weathering of a sample of material under 
the influence of light, oxidation, moisture, and other 
weather parameters. 


Example: Xenon Arc or EMMAQUA. 
4 CLASSIFICATIONS OF CLADDING FILMS 


4.1 According to Use 


For the purpose of this standard, according to their uses, 
the cladding films for greenhouses shall be classified as 
given in Table 1. 


IS 15827 : 2019 


5 MATERIALS 


Cladding multilayer films for greenhouses shall be 
manufactured as from the following polymers: 


a) Low density polyethylene (LDPE), linear low 
density polyethylene (LLDPE) and their blends; 


b) Ethylene vinyl acetate copolymers (E/VAC) and 
their blends with LDPE or LLDPE; 


c) Ethylene butyl-acrylate copolymers (E/BA) and 
their blends with LDPE or LLDPE; and 


d) UV stabilizers, master batches and other additives 
for desired properties like UV blocking, diffusion, 
anti-drip, thermal, IR cooling, anti-dust, anti- 
sulphur, anti-mist / fog. 


6 REQUIREMENTS 


6.1 Appearance 


The film shall be uniform in colour, texture and finish. 
The film shall be free from pinholes and undispersed 
raw materials, streaks and particles of foreign matter. 
There shall be no other visible defects, such as holes, 
tears or blisters. The edges shall be free from nicks and 
cuts visible to unaided eye. 


6.2 Durability (Resistance to Artificial Weathering) 


The duration of a covering film shall be 36 months 
as declared by the manufacturer and is determined by 
testing the variation of its elongation at break after 
accelerated weathering according to the method given 
in 7.5. 


6.3 Specific requirements of cladding film shall be as 
given in Table 2. 


7 TEST METHODS 


7.1 Appearance 


The free edges of the roll shall be sealed with adhesive 
tape or by some other similar means, in order to prevent 
its unwinding. The edges should be properly in line and 
there should be sufficient tens ion to prevent the layer of

the roll from transverse slipping when it is handled (this 
should be done horizontally). The film shall be checked 
by unrolling at least 2 m of the film and examining it 
against the light at arm’s length. 


7.2 Determination of Width 


7.2.1 Unroll the film or sheeting into lap form in such 
a way that the length of each lap does not exceed 5 m, 
and that there are no more than twenty laps directly one 
above the other. Allow the material in the lap form for at 
least 1 h before the measurements are made. In case of 
non-rolled samples, 30 min conditioning is sufficient. 


7.2.2 Lay the film on a flat surface having about 10 m 
length and at least as wide as the film to be measured. 
Place the scale subdivided into 1 mm divisions on the 
film in such a manner that it is at right angles to the 
length direction of the film. With zero mark on the scale 
aligned squarely with the left longitudinal edge of the 
film. Determine the exact position of the right edge of 
the material on the scale to the nearest 1 mm and record 
the result. 


7.2.3 The number of measurements to be made 
depends on the overall length of the roll or sample 
to be inspected. For length upto 5 m, determine the 
width at least three times along the sample length at 
approximately equal intervals. For length longer than 
5 m, determine the width at least ten times along the 
length at approximately equal intervals. 


7.2.4 Record the width measured and report the 
arithmetic mean as the average width of the roll or 


sample. However for actual use, the smallest width be 
considered if one piece material is to be used. 


7.3 Elongation Under a Steady Load (Creep Test) 
7.3.1 Principle 


To measure the elongation of a film under a stated load 
after a fixed time in a vertical static position. 
7.3.2 Apparatus 
Two grips hold the test specimen. A weight is hung to 
the lower (free) grip to provide a steady stress in the 
specimen. The upper grip is clamped to a fixed support: 
7.3.3 Operative Conditions 
The test shall be done on 3 specimens cut from the film 
in the machine direction (MD). 
7.3.3.1 Dimension of the specimen 

a) Width: 10 mm, 

b) Total length: 140 mm, and 

c) Gauge length defined between two marks: 

100 mm. 


7.3.3.2 Test conditions 


a) Test temperature: 27 + 2°C, 
b) Load to be applied: 4 Mpa, and 
c) Duration of test: 100 h. 


7.3.4 Procedure 


Place the test specimen on which the gauge length of 
100 mm has been marked in the grips. Calculate the 


weight which is needed for the test with reference to 
the minimum cross-section of the specimen and adjust 
the test weight to this value (for example by adding 
or removing lead shot to the weight). Carefully hang 
the system, grips — specimen — weight to the fixed 
support, avoiding jerks and shocks. 
NOTE — During the test the apparatus shall not be subjected to 
vibration or shocks which may influence the final measurement. 
Maintenance and temperature during entire period of test be 
ensured. 


7.3.5 Results 


The results are expressed as the strain of the sample as 
a percentage of the original length. 
L-Li 
Li 


A= x 100 


Where, 
A= value of the creep; 
Li= initial gauge length, in mm; and 
L= arithmetic mean of the medium final distance 


between the two marks that define the gauge 
length of each specimen. 


7.4 IR Effectiveness — Barrier against Thermic 
Radiation 


7.4.1 Principle 


The method consists of measuring the IR transmission 
spectrum of thermic film within wave numbers ranging 
from 1 430 cm”! to 770 cm" (between 7 um and 13 um 
wavelengths). 


This range of wavelengths corresponds to the field 
of maximum emission of the energy radiated by the 
earth’s surface. 


7.4.2 Apparatus 


Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscope (FTIR) or 
Infrared spectrophotometer with a recorder. Analytical 
balance with a 0.1 mg margin of error or planimeter. 


7.4.3 Procedure 


The measurement shall be done on 5 specimens taken 
from the film under test. Put each specimen to be checked 
on the specimen holder of the spectrophotometer and 
record the spectrum of transmission from 1 430 cm! 
to 770 cm”. Measure the area between 100 percent 
transmittance and the curve of the spectrum with the 
help of a planimeter or by using the weighing method 
given in 7.4.3.1. 


7.4.3.1 Weighing method 


Cut a sheet bearing the trace of the spectrum (or a copy 
of it) at 1430 cm? and 770 cm" and along the lines 
of 0 percent and 100 percent transmittance. Weigh this 
rectangle to an accuracy of 0.1 mg. This mass shall be 
stated as P,,,. Then cut along the outline of the spectrum 
and weigh the part representing the transmission. This 
second mass shall be stated as P 


IS 15827 : 2019 


7.4.4 Setting Out the Results 
7.4.4.1 Planimeter method 


The percentage of the measured area of the spectrum 
in respect to the total area is the value of the IR 
effectiveness. 


7.4.4.2 Weighing method 


The IR absorption in the range of wavelengths between 

7 to 13 mm is given by the following formula: 

IR = P100-P1 
P100 


x 100 


effectiveness 


7.5 Resistance to Artificial Weathering 


7.5.1 Principle 


This measurement involves determining the variation 
of elongation at break of the film after exposure to a 
xenon arc light source that simulates the spectral power 
distribution of solar light in accordance with IS 13360 
(Part 9/Sec 5). The sample of the films shall be irradiated 
according to 7.5.3. After irradiation, the elongation is 
determined on five rectangular specimens, 10 mm wide 
and 150 mm long taken longitudinally (MD), according 
to IS 13360 (Part 5/Sec 3). 


7.5.2 Apparatus 


The apparatus shall consist of xenon arc sources with 
a double filter borosilicate for simulating the direct 
sunlight [see IS 13360 (Part 9/Sec 5)]. 


7.5.3 Test Conditions 


a) The irradiance at the wave length of 340 nm shall 
be fixed at 0.35 W/m2 nm. In this condition the 
irradiance in the visible range (300 nm to 800 nm) 
should be about 400 W/m2, 


b) Spray cycle: 


1) duration of spraying: 18 + 0.5 min, 


2) dry interval between spraying: 102 + 0.5 min, 
c) Black standard temperature (65 + 3°C) , and 
d) Relative humidity (65 + 5 percent). 


7.5.4 Procedure 


A sample of film shall be irradiated according to 7.5.3. 
After irradiation, the elongation at break shall be 
determined according to Table 3 using test specimens 
Type 2, 10 mm wide, taken longitudinally (MD) with 
a speed of 500 mm/min in accordance with the test 
procedure given in IS 13360 (Part 5/Sec 1). 


7.5.5 Results 


The arithmetic mean of the 5 measurements is 
calculated, and compared to the value of the Elongation 
at break of Table 2, depending on the type of the film. 
The duration is in accordance with the considered class 
when the arithmetic mean is equal or greater than 50 
percent of the value given in Table 2. 


IS 15827 : 2019 


Table 3 Minimum Duration of Exposure 


Class Minimum duration of exposure (h)

8 MARKING 8.3 BIS Certification Marking 


8.1 The film shall be indelibly marked along the 
edges with permanent black ink on every meter with 
following information:- 


a) Manufacturer’s name and recognized trademark, 
if any; 
b) Type of the film, as per Table 1; 
c) Thickness of the film; 
d) Batch number and date of manufacture; 
e) Symbol for recycle; and 
f) Inside / Outside layer identification 
8.2 The width, length, weight, thickness and class of 


the roll/folded film shall be mentioned on packing slip/ 
sticker. 


The film may also be marked with the BIS Standard 
Mark. 


8.3.1 The use of the Standard Mark is governed by the 
provisions of Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 2016 
and the Rules and Regulations made there under. The 
details of the conditions under which the licence for use 
of the Standard Mark may be granted to manufacturers 
or producers may be obtained from the Bureau of 
Indian Standards.

Review of Indian Standards 


Amendments are issued to standards as the need arises on the basis of comments. Standards are also reviewed 
periodically; a standard along with amendments is reaffirmed when such review indicates that no changes are 
needed; if the review indicates that changes are needed, it is taken up for revision. Users of Indian Standards 
should ascertain that they are in possession of the latest amendments or edition by referring to the latest issue of 
‘BIS Catalogue’ and ‘Standards: Monthly Additions’. 


This Indian Standard has been developed from Doc No.: FAD 20 (12791).
